content: A multibacillary (MB) case of leprosy is defined as a condition where the patient has more than five skin lesions, nerve involvement (such as pure neuritis or any number of skin lesions accompanied by neuritis), or the presence of bacilli detected in a slit-skin smear, regardless of the number of skin lesions. Early diagnosis and complete treatment using multidrug therapy (MDT) are critical strategies for reducing the burden of leprosy. Standard MDT regimens for paucibacillary (PB) and MB leprosy were introduced in 1982. For PB leprosy, the treatment involves two drugs for six months, while MB leprosy initially required a minimum of 24 months of treatment, which was later reduced to 12 months in 1998 based on recommendations from the WHO Expert Committee. MDT is provided in blister packs, each containing four weeks of treatment. Separate blister packs are available for MB and PB leprosy, with different dosages for adults and children. The standard adult treatment regimen for MB leprosy includes rifampicin (600 mg once a month), clofazimine (300 mg once a month and 50 mg daily), and dapsone (100 mg daily) for a duration of 12 months (12 blister packs of 28 days each). For PB leprosy, the adult regimen includes rifampicin (600 mg once a month) and dapsone (100 mg daily) for six months (6 blister packs of 28 days each). For children aged 10–14 years, the MB regimen includes rifampicin (450 mg once a month), clofazimine (150 mg once a month and 50 mg every other day), and dapsone (50 mg daily) for 12 months. The PB regimen for children includes rifampicin (450 mg once a month) and dapsone (50 mg daily) for six months. MDT is provided free of charge globally through an agreement between a pharmaceutical company and WHO. WHO manages the distribution of MDT in collaboration with national leprosy programs. While WHO has not issued specific recommendations on preventive strategies, research on various antibiotics and their combinations has been ongoing since the 1990s. A WHO guideline for leprosy is needed to address demands from member states for proper guidance in specific program areas and to incorporate new evidence. The last WHO guidance on leprosy was issued in 2010, with the previous one in 1998. A new guideline is also necessary to address clinical uncertainties in the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of leprosy. Early diagnosis, particularly of PB leprosy, remains a challenge, and a diagnostic test for early detection could be a key tool for preventing transmission, initiating early treatment, and reducing disabilities caused by leprosy. Although prevention is preferable to treating clinical disease, prior WHO guidance has not addressed prevention. In the absence of WHO evidence-based guidelines, some countries have developed their own policies on prevention. Drug-resistant leprosy has been identified in several countries, but there is no recent WHO guidance on its treatment. Surveillance guidelines for monitoring drug resistance in leprosy were issued by WHO in 2009 and updated in 2017. Therefore, updated guidelines are needed to address treatment for leprosy, including the use of standard MDT regimens for PB and MB leprosy, as well as alternative approaches such as uniform MDT (UMDT), which uses the same three-drug, six-month regimen for both PB and MB leprosy. The target audience for these guidelines includes policymakers in ministries of health, medical staff in lowand middle-income countries, and NGOs providing leprosy services. The guidelines aim to assist in the development of national leprosy plans and provide recommendations on current diagnostic tools, drug combinations for treatment, and preventive chemotherapy. They are also intended to help clinicians treating leprosy patients, researchers by identifying gaps in research, and donors in prioritizing funding. The overall goal of these guidelines is to provide evidence-based recommendations for the diagnosis, treatment, and prevention of leprosy, with a focus on the use of antibiotics for chemoprophylaxis. The primary audience includes policymakers and clinicians managing leprosy, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. The development of these guidelines involved contributions from various groups, including the WHO Steering Group, the Guidelines Development Group (GDG), and external contributors. The Steering Group included experts in leprosy, disease control, intellectual property, essential medicines evaluation, neglected tropical diseases (NTDs), and gender, equity, and human rights. The GDG met twice, once in New Delhi, India, in May 2017, and once via teleconference in October 2017, to review additional evidence and finalize recommendations. External contributors included a systematic review team led by Dr. Amudha Poobalan from Aberdeen University, UK, and an External Review Group (ERG) composed of individuals with expertise in leprosy and health program implementation. The ERG identified errors, commented on clarity, and highlighted issues for implementation but did not modify the recommendations. The ERG included persons affected by leprosy and experts in stigma and discrimination related to communicable diseases. The guideline development process adhered to WHO policies for managing conflicts of interest. All potential members submitted declarations of interest, which were reviewed by the GLP Team Leader and the Office of Compliance, Risk Management, and Ethics. No individual was excluded from participation due to conflicts of interest. Key questions guiding the systematic review were developed using the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcomes) format. These questions addressed leprosy diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. For example, one question explored whether a single uniform treatment regimen for all leprosy patients is as effective and safe as the current separate regimens for PB and MB leprosy. Systematic reviews were conducted by an independent reviewer commissioned by WHO, with oversight from the Steering Group and methodologist. Literature searches were performed in databases such as Embase, MEDLINE, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials. Data extraction and risk of bias assessments were conducted using standardized tools. Meta-analysis was not performed due to the small number of studies and methodological limitations. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE method, which categorizes evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low. Recommendations were formulated based on the evidence, considering factors such as benefits, harms, feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and values and preferences of end users. Recommendations were graded as strong or conditional based on the confidence in the balance of benefits and harms. Patient perspectives were incorporated through surveys and focus group discussions conducted in four countries (Colombia, Ghana, India, and Nepal). These discussions highlighted barriers such as stigma, lack of trained staff, and health system issues. Suggestions for improvement included better counseling, community education, and integration of preventive treatment into existing health campaigns. The guidelines also considered human rights impacts, including effects on family life, employment, education, and healthcare.
